title: Soap & Candle Calculator — lye, superfat and wax
description: A cold-process soap calculator: pick eleven common oils by weight, choose NaOH or KOH, set the superfat, water (lye concentration, water:lye ratio or % of oils) and fragrance rate, and get what to weigh out, to 0.1 g or 0.01 oz. The SAP values are SoapCalc's, cross-checked against three more published charts with the four-source range shown, and KOH values are derived as NaOH × 56.1/40. A container-candle tab works out wax and fragrance from the jar's volume, fill level and a stated wax density. A lye safety notice that can't be dismissed sits above the results.
prompt: Build a soap and candle calculator where accuracy and safety come first. For cold-process soap, let me pick common oils by weight from a table with their NaOH and KOH SAP values, cross-checked against more than one reputable soap-making reference and cited on the page. Compute the lye with a superfat (default 5%), water as a lye concentration or water:lye ratio, and fragrance at a usage rate. For candles, work out the wax from the container volume and fill level (state the wax density you use), the fragrance load, and add a wick note that says test burns are required. Put a prominent safety notice in the lye section that can't be hidden: lye into water never the reverse, goggles and gloves, ventilation, keep away from children, no aluminium, weigh everything, and double-check with an established lye calculator. Never present the output as guaranteed safe. Tests should check the lye math against hand-computed recipes, the KOH conversion, every water mode, rounding, unit conversions and that the safety notice can't be hidden.

methodology: Hand-computed oracles: the spec holds its own SoapCalc NaOH table and computes lye = Σ(oil weight × SAP) × (1 − superfat) for three recipes (the 1000 g sample, which comes to exactly 140.6 g, a lard and coconut recipe at 7%, and an ounce recipe), then compares the page's rounded text.

Published values as the reference: all four charts' figures are typed into the spec (Voyageur's mg KOH/g converted × 40/56.1), and the test recomputes the min–max range for each oil. It checks that the page's range column agrees and that the value used sits inside it. Derived KOH values must land within 1% of SoapCalc's own KOH column.

Every water mode is checked against its formula: concentration c gives water = lye × (100 − c)/c, ratio r gives lye × r, and % of oils gives oils × p. The page's concentration and ratio readouts must be consistent with each mode.

Units: exact conversion constants (1 oz = 28.349523125 g, 1 US fl oz = 29.5735295625 mL), rounding to 0.1 g and 0.01 oz, recipes typed in ounces, and switching back to grams without drift, because the page stores grams internally.

Safety: the notice's required phrases, no control inside it, not in a details or dialog element, above the results, and still visible after Escape, every mode change and a tab round-trip. The spec also checks the 'not a guarantee' disclaimer and the wick-test note.
risks: SAP values vary between lots of the same oil. Coconut has the widest spread across the four sources, 0.183–0.191, about 4%. The 5% default superfat covers that, but a user who sets 0% could get lye-heavy soap. The page warns about that; the calculator can't prevent it.

KOH purity differs by supplier (often about 90%). The default is 100%, so the result is the plain SAP figure; a user with 90% KOH who leaves the default gets slightly less lye, which errs on the soft, not caustic, side.
Candle fragrance is treated as a % of wax weight, with the same density as wax. Some suppliers quote load as a % of the total, which gives slightly different numbers; the page states its convention.
Soap quality numbers were left out on purpose: they need fatty-acid profiles that aren't sourced here.
qa.playwright: Web-first toHaveText assertions against strings the spec formats itself (toFixed(1) + ' g') made the rounding checks exact without reading any page internals. check() drives the radio groups and selectOption the candle unit. The safety test uses boundingBox to prove the notice sits above the results, and a locator count of zero for buttons, links, inputs and summary elements inside it to prove there's nothing to close it with. keyboard.press checks Escape and arrow-key tab switching. Candidly, every test passed on its first run, so this spec hasn't caught a regression yet. Its value is that the oracle tables are independent copies of the published charts: a typo in the page's SAP table would fail the first test. Playwright can't check that soap made with these numbers is safe, which is why the page tells people to confirm with an established calculator.
coverage: SAP table vs SoapCalc; four-source ranges; KOH = NaOH × 56.1/40
Lye for three hand-computed recipes; superfat; KOH purity
Water by concentration, ratio and % of oils; fragrance; batch total
Grams and ounces, rounding, typing in ounces, no drift on switching
Non-dismissable lye notice, disclaimer, warnings for 0% superfat, out-of-range values and no oils
Candle wax and fragrance in mL and US fl oz, multiple jars, density stated, wick note, keyboard tabs

a11y: Every input is a labelled native field, and units, lye type and water method are radio groups in fieldsets with legends. The soap and candle views are an ARIA tablist with arrow-key switching and roving tabindex. Results and warnings are polite live regions, and the lye safety notice is a labelled note that is always in the reading order before the results. Clearing the oils moves focus to the first weight field.
